## Methods

Materials
The raw materials are shown as follows: poly (vinyl alcohol) (MW= 89000~98000, 95%), CuSO4 (MW=159.61, 99%), Cu(NO3)2.xH2O (MW=187.56, 99.0%), Na2SO4 (MW=142.04, 99.5%), KCl (MW=74.55, 99.5%), CaCl2 (MW=110.98, 99.99%), MgCl2 (MW=95.21, 99.99%), CuCl2 (MW=134.45, 98%), ZnCl2 (MW=136.3, 99.95%), CoCl2.6H2O (MW=237.93, 99.99%), NiCl2 (MW=129.6, 99%) were provided by Macklin Biochemical CO., Ltd. NaCl (MW=58.44, 99.5%), AlCl3 (MW=133.34, 99%) were purchased from Aladdin Industrial Corporation. Carbon paper (TGP-H-060) was purchased from Toray Industries. Inc. (Japan).

Preparation of PVA hydrogel
The PVA hydrogel was prepared by using the freeze-thaw method. In this work, we regulated the weight ratio of PVA to water (rw = 7.5%, 10%, 12.5%, and 15%). As an example, for preparing 10 wt% PVA hydrogel, 6 g of PVA powder was first dissolved and stirred in 54 mL DI water for 30 min. Then, the PVA solution was heated and stirred in a water bath at 95°C for 6 h. Finally, the as-prepared solution was defoamed and poured into a mold (size: 15mm×15mm×3mm (length×width×height)), frozen at −20°C for 6 h and thawed at 25°C for 1 h, repeating three times, to obtain the PVA hydrogel. The mold was prepared by using the Bambu Lab X1E 3D printer.

Preparation of PVA-based i-TE gels
The general formula of the i-TE gels was PVA(rw)-xMX (x: the molar concentration of MX salts; MX = NaCl, KCl, CuSO4, Cu(NO3)2, CuCl2, CaCl2, ZnCl2, MgCl2, CoCl2, NiCl2, and AlCl3). All the i-TE gels in this work were prepared via immersing the PVA hydrogels in the corresponding salt solutions. As an example, for preparing the PVA (10 wt.%)- 1.5/0.25M CuCl2/CaCl2 i-TE gel: firstly, the 10 wt.% PVA hydrogel was prepared as the above method; then 4.034 g CuCl2 and 0.555 g CaCl2 were dissolved into 20 mL DI water to obtain the mixture salt solution; finally, the PVA hydrogel was immersed in the solution for 12 h and obtained the i-TE gel.

Fabrication of i-TE cells
Carbon paper was used as the electrodes for assembling the i-TE cells with a 3 mm-thick sandwich structure CP|i-TE gel|CP. The size of the as-prepared i-TE gel is 15mm×15mm×3mm, and the size of the carbon paper is 25×25mm. The cell molds are identical to those used in the PVA preparation process. To optimize the output power, gold-coated carbon paper was also employed as electrodes46. Gold (Au) sputtering on the carbon paper was conducted using a Denton Vacuum Desktop Pro system at an argon pressure of 20 mTorr and an operating power of 120W for 40s, resulting in a film thickness of approximately 40 nm. The as-fabricated i-TE cell was encapsulated in a polyethylene film using a hot press machine to prevent the gel from losing water.

Fabrication of the i-TE module
The 16-cell module was assembled in series using titanium (Ti) taps. The size of each i-TE unit was 10mm×10mm×3mm, which can be uniformed prepared by the 3D-printed molds. The size of Au@CP and the CP electrode was 11×11mm. The as-fabricated i-TE module was encapsulated in a polyethylene film using a hot press machine. The temperature difference was generated by the heat plate and the semiconductor cooling platform. Other performance tests are the same as those of the i-TE cell.

Ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) spectroscopy (Integrating Sphere) characterization
The Ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) spectroscopy was conducted on an Agilent Cary 5000 spectrometer using an integral ball accessory. The absorption signals of UV-vis are always unlimited when the CuCl2 concentrations are higher than 0.1M. Herein, an integrating sphere was employed to select the diffuse reflection signals of i-TE gels and then to achieve the corresponding absorption intensity. The size of the gels is 15mm×15mm×0.5mm. In this work, all the UV-vis spectra of the gels were obtained by using this method.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) characterization
The XPS test was conducted on a Thermo-Scientific Escalab QXi microprobe. The gels were immediately taken out from the i-TE cells after thermal charging with a ΔT of 10 K for 30 min and freeze-dried for 48 h to obtain the dried samples. A ΔT of 10 K was constructed from the bottom to the top across the i-TE gel. The gel top is near the cold side of the electrode (TC) while the gel bottom is near the hot side of the electrode (TH).

X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) characterization
The XANES spectra at Cu K-edge were performed at BL11B beamline of Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The data were obtained under ambient conditions in fluorescence mode for the Cu K-edge. The gel sample is a freeze-dried PVA-0.1M CuCl2 gel that has been thermally charged for 30 min. The CuO and Cu2O were used as the standard samples to confirm the copper electron states in the i-TE gel.

Operando Raman spectra characterization
The Xplora confocal microprobe Raman system (HORIBA) was used to record the Raman spectra. All measurements were performed using a He-Ne laser with an excitation wavelength of 637.8 nm and a 50x long working distance (8mm) microscope objective with a numerical aperture of 0.55. The Raman frequency was calibrated using a silicon wafer in each experiment. In this study, PVA-CuCl2 gels containing different concentrations of CuCl2 (0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, and 1 M) were placed in a specially designed temperature-controlled Raman cell for operando testing of the gel surface and cross-sections. The temperature difference was controlled at 10 K, crossing from the bottom to the top in the gel top surface test, and from left to right in the cross-section test, respectively. The humidity was maintained at 60%. In addition, PVA-0.01M CuCl2 gel was soaked in heavy water (D2O) for 12 h, and isotopes were used to confirm that the peak at 420 cm−1 is the Cu-O stretching vibration of [Cu-H2O]. Here, we defined a normalized [Cu-Cl] factor to quantify the coordination species change. For the original state of PVA-0.1M CuCl2 i-TE gels, the Raman peak from 215.2 to 296.5 cm−1 of [Cu-Cl] species, and the corresponding integration area was 11717. We defined the [Cu-Cl] factor of this state as 1. The factors at different reaction times could be calculated by making a ratio between the integrated [Cu-Cl] peak area with 11717. Taking PVA-0.1M CuCl2 gel as an example, as the thermal charging time increased from 5 to 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 mins, the integrated [Cu-Cl] Raman peak area was 13357, 16404, 23786, 31402, 36557, and 41947, respectively, corresponding to the normalized [Cu-Cl] factor increased from 1 to 1.14, 1.40, 2.03, 2.68, 3.12, and 3.58. The normalized [Cu-Cl] factors of others samples with different CuCl2 concentrations were achieved by using the same method.

Electrochemical characterization
The electrochemical characterization, including Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) test, was measured on an electrochemical workstation (Admiral Instruments, America). For aqueous salt solutions, CV test scanning from −0.6 V to +0.8 V was conducted with a three-electrode configuration, carbon paper (size: 1.5cm×1.5cm) was used as the working electrode and platinum (size: 1cm×1cm) and Ag/AgCl electrodes were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. 2M Na2SO4 was employed as the supporting electrolyte in aqueous media to reduce the ohmic overpotential. For symmetrical i-TE cells, CV test scanning from −0.6 and +0.6V was conducted with a two-electrode configuration, in which one carbon paper electrode served as the working electrode while another was employed as the counter and reference electrodes simultaneously. The EIS was adopted to analyze the resistance properties of the cells between 0.05 Hz to 10000 Hz at the AC amplitude of 10 mV. The ionic conductivities of gels were calculated using Eq. 1

σ = l / RS (1)

where l, S, and R are the thickness, the cross-sectional area, and the resistance of the i-TE cells, respectively. The R is the first interception of the high-frequency semicircle (fitted Rs) in the results of the EIS measurement.

I-TE performance measurement. The ionic thermoelectric performance was measured using an Ionic Thermoelectric Testing System (ITTS, PURI Materials). The thermal voltage (ΔV) and temperature difference (ΔT) were recorded using a built-in test program. Thermopower was the slope of ΔV versus ΔT. The thermopower (Si) was calculated according to Eq. 2:

Si = (V(TH) - V(TC)) / ΔT (2)

Where Si is the thermopower, V(TH) and V(TC) are the potential at the hot side and cold sides of the i-TE cells, respectively. TH and TC are the temperatures at the hot and cold sides of the i-TE cells, respectively. The ΔT was set to 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5K, and the cold side (TC) was maintained at 298.15K.

The instantaneous output power was measured using a Keithley-2400 at a voltage-current (V-I) discharge at a ΔT of 10 K. TC was fixed at 298.15K. For normalized maximum power density, the distance between the two electrodes was 0.3 cm, and the cross-sectional area of the electrode was 2.25 cm−2. The normalized instantaneous output power density (Pmax) was calculated according to Eq. 3:

Pmax = Voc * Isc / 4 (3)

Where Voc and Isc are the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit density, respectively.

The continuous output voltage and current were measured using the ITTS at a ΔT of 10 K. TC was fixed at 298.15K. The energy density (E) was calculated according to Eq. 4:

E = ∫0t V(t)I(t)dt (4)

Where the V(t) and I(t) are the output voltage and current dependent on t, t is the output power time.

### Reviewer 1

This study reports that the competitive-coupling effect, driven by speciation, facilitates the development of high-performance and sustainable n-type ionic thermoelectric (i-TE) cells. The authors identified a novel n-type redox couple, Cu²⁺/Cu⁺, stabilized by Cl⁻ ions, and demonstrated a competitive-coupling i-TE mechanism, driven by speciation, in polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-CuCl₂ gels. This mechanism enhances the thermogalvanic effect while suppressing the thermodiffusion of Cl⁻ ions as CuCl₂ concentration increases. By modulating ion-coordination speciation, the system achieves a substantial thermopower of -30.6 mV K⁻¹ and an outstanding power density of 0.6 mW m⁻² K⁻². Furthermore, a 16-cell module generates a thermal voltage of 3.5 V and an output power of 22 µW under a temperature difference (ΔT) of 15 K. While the research topic is intriguing, the evidence supporting the competitive-coupling i-TE mechanism is insufficient. Several critical issues require major revision:
(1) The "competitive-coupling" mechanism proposed by the authors in the article is essentially a linear superposition of the Soret and thermogalvanic effects, weighted by ionic concentration. It may be more accurate to characterize this as a synergistic effect modulated by ion concentration.
(2) To establish a correlation between coordination species changes and valence states, the authors employed SHINERS alongside XPS mapping of Cu²⁺ and Cu⁺ distribution near the gel surface. However, given that XPS sampling is limited to a few nanometers, while ion migration in gels occurs on the micrometer scale, it is advisable to supplement the analysis with Cu K-edge XANES. This would confirm whether the valence state distribution observed at the surface is representative of the bulk gel.
(3) In the main text on page 8, Fig. 3c and Fig. 3d are cited out of sequence and should be swapped to align with their actual order in Fig. 3.
(4) The thermoelectric conversion efficiency should be included to provide a comprehensive evaluation of i-TE cell performance.
(5) The reported energy density and operating time (2 h) are not particularly remarkable. A longer-duration test is essential for practical applications, particularly in self-powered wearable sensors.
(6) In this section, the authors increased the redox couple concentration by enriching Cl⁻ content, achieving an optimized Pmax with 0.25 M CaCl₂. However, it remains unclear whether Ca²⁺ participates in coordination or merely exerts an ionic-strength effect.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript reports the development of a high-performance n-type i-TE material by coupling two synergistic effects. The i-TE material is the hot research spot of the field, especially the high-performance n-type ones. This work is well prepared by exploring new way to improve the i-TE performance with both experimental tests and theoretical simulation. I would recommend its publication. Below are some comments to improve the quality.
(1) Photos of fabricated samples, and corresponding structure, composition and morphology characterization as well as mechanical properties upon varying key component contents are needed, to prove the achievement of the material. This also applies to the i-TE device with close look at the details the device such as the size and the thickness.
(2) Drying of hydrogel is a key issue hindering the practical long-term use. How does the developed one dry over time, and is there any anti-drying treatment used?
(3) Cycling charge-discharge test of the assembled i-TE cells is only done with 10 cycles, which is too small. More cycles are needed, to verify the repeatability and consistence.

### Reviewer 3

The authors report a CuCl₂-based binary ionic thermoelectric (i-TE) system in which Cl⁻ ions are proposed to regulate the coupling between interfacial redox reactions and bulk thermodiffusion, leading to a reported thermopower of −30.6 mV K⁻¹. The work combines experimental thermopower characterization with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to rationalize the distribution of Cu–Cl–H₂O complexes. The topic is timely and relevant to the expanding field of ionic thermoelectrics, and the data appear internally consistent.
However, the mechanistic interpretation and novelty require substantial clarification. The reported transient current profiles, limited thermogalvanic (TG) quantification, and incomplete benchmarking against the state of the art raise significant questions about the claimed TG-dominated mechanism. Substantial revision, including direct quantification of the TG contribution, clarified novelty, and improved benchmarking, would be necessary for to justify publication in this journal.
1. Novelty and Relation to Previous Work: The claimed TG-in-TD mechanism is conceptually similar to prior reports: eg. Han et al., Science 2020, 368, 1091–1098 and Zeng et al., Adv. Energy Mater. 2023, 13, 2204357. Both studies describe synergistic thermodiffusion and thermogalvanic contributions producing large thermopower. Although the current materials differ in composition (n-type), the mechanistic framework and observed behavior appear analogous. The authors should clearly delineate what is genuinely new in this work—whether in chemical design, redox kinetics, or thermodynamic coupling—and avoid implying a fundamentally new mechanism without quantitative differentiation.
2. Transient versus Steady-State Current Behavior: The long-term current–voltage data (Supporting Fig. 34) display sharp transient spikes that rapidly decay to near zero, rather than steady currents under ΔT. This response is typical of thermodiffusion-dominated systems, not TG-driven ones. If a true thermogalvanic process were dominant, a sustained redox-driven current would persist as long as the temperature gradient remains, as in the TG + TD system of Han et al. (Science 2020, 368, 1091–1098). The combination of transient decay and low open-circuit voltage relative to Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ redox potentials weakens the mechanistic conclusion. The authors should provide quantitative TG validation e.g., steady-state current monitoring, or equivalent circuit separation of ionic vs. redox contributions.
3. Interpretation of “Simultaneous High Current and Voltage”: The claim of achieving both large current output and high voltage is misleading. The CuCl₂-based gel cannot transport electrons internally; current appears only when an external load provides an electronic pathway. The authors should correct this statement to specify that current flow arises from external-circuit conduction, not from intrinsic electronic transport in the gel.
4. Quantitative Estimation of TG Contribution: While the XPS results suggest Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ redox involvement, peak-area ratios cannot be directly correlated with current density or Seebeck enhancement. Without quantitative estimation of the TG fraction, the mechanistic claim remains speculative. Given the non-sustained current profile, the system appears thermodiffusion-dominated with a limited or transient TG component. The authors should revisit the data interpretation and possibly reframe the paper around TD-enhanced ionic thermopower rather than TG dominance.
5. Comparison with the State of the Art: Figure 1f and Supporting Table 1 and 2 omit key recent references. For example, a recent report in Energy & Environmental Science (Energy Environ. Sci., 2025,18, 1294-1309) achieved thermopower exceeding −40 mV K⁻¹ at ΔT = 5.3 K. Accordingly, the statement “Binary PVA–CuCl₂ gels exhibit remarkable advantages in thermopower and output performance compared to other reported multicomponent n-type i-TE systems” is overstated and should be revised. Comprehensive benchmarking with the latest literature is required for an accurate contextual comparison.
6. Power Density Discrepancy: The reported power density of this work (binary PVA–CuCl₂ gel) is orders of magnitude lower than comparable systems: For eg. Adv. Energy Mater. 2023 , 13, 2204357. The authors should discuss the physical origin of this low performance—e.g., internal resistance, poor interfacial kinetics, or limited ionic–electronic coupling—and provide quantitative reasoning for why the binary PVA–CuCl₂ gel performs so modestly despite the large thermopower.
